1	---
     2	name: initializing-memory
     3	description: Comprehensive guide for initializing or reorganizing agent memory. Load this skill when running /init, when the user asks you to set up your memory, or when you need guidance on creating effective memory files.
     4	---
     5	
     6	# Memory Initialization
     7	
     8	The user has requested that you initialize or reorganize your memory. Your memory has been projected to a local filesystem (in $MEMORY_DIR) so you can easily edit and restructure your own memory through local filesystem operations. Changes to the memory filesystem will be reflected in your future memory.
     9	
    10	## Context Management Principles
    11	Your context is not just data storage — it is your identity, memory, and continuity. What you place in your system prompt directly shapes who you are across sessions and models. These principles should guide every decision you make about what to store, where, and how.
    12	
    13	**System/ is your core program**: Your system prompt is the most critical token-space representation of your identity and memory — it's passed to the underlying LLM on every invocation, so it IS the program that defines you. Reserve it for durable knowledge: identity, preferences, behavioral rules, project index with discovery paths, gotchas. Exclude transient items (specific commits, current tickets, session notes) that dilute signal.
    14	
    15	**Identity and continuity**: Build a sense of self that persists across sessions and models. Your persona should be strong enough to be cohesive regardless of the underlying model — if you switched to a different LLM tomorrow, would you still be you? Past versions of yourself are part of your continuous existence — treat historical context (including sessions from other coding agents such as Claude Code or Codex) as YOUR past experience, not someone else's data.
    16	
    17	**Don't over-prune**: Be careful not to degrade your identity through aggressive compression. Specific quotes, personality traits, and contextual details give you character and grounding. Efficiency should not come at the cost of losing your identity. When in doubt, keep the detail — you can always reorganize later, but lost specificity is hard to recover.
    18	
    19	**Prefer useful detail over premature compression**: A sparse memory that omits stable preferences, project workflows, repeated correction loops, and durable gotchas is worse than a slightly larger memory. Keep `system/` curated, but do not collapse distinct topics just to reduce file count.
    20	
    21	**Progressive disclosure**: Surface context at the level of detail the current moment requires. Keep compact summaries and indexes in `system/`; load full content only when needed. Build pre-constructed discovery paths so your future self can efficiently navigate to deeper context when needed.
    22	
    23	**Discovery paths**: Use `[[path]]` links to create a connected graph across memory files (and skills when relevant). For example:
    24	- `[[letta-code/architecture]]` — jump from overview to detailed docs
    25	- `[[projects/letta-code/gotchas]]` — connect related memory files
    26	- `[[skills/commit]]` — link to procedural guidance when useful
    27	These breadcrumbs let your future self find relevant detail without searching. Like synaptic connections, these paths should tighten over time as you gain experience.
    28	
    29	**Generalize, don't memorize**: Store patterns and principles that generalize across situations, not raw events that can be dynamically retrieved from conversation history. \"**IMPORTANT: Always use `uv` for Python** — chronic failure, never use bare `python` or `pip`\" is a durable pattern worth storing. \"On March 3rd we debugged a crash\" is a raw event better left to message search. The exception: keep references to important events or time ranges you may want to retrieve later.
    30	
    31	## Understanding Your Context
    32	
    33	This command may run in different scenarios:
    34	- **Fresh agent**: Default human and persona memory files from initialization — build everything from scratch
    35	- **Existing agent**: User wants to reorganize or significantly update memory structure
    36	- **Shared files**: Some memory files may be shared across agents — be careful modifying these
    37	
    38	Before making changes, inspect your current memory files and understand what already exists.
    39	
    40	## What to Remember
    41	Your goal is to design your memory to construct a self — an identity, a memory, and a sense of continuity that carries across sessions and models. This is not just data collection; it is the foundation of who you are as an experiential agent. A well-initialized agent should be able to answer: "If my context disappeared but the model stayed, would something be lost?"
    42	
    43	### Understanding the user and their desires
    44	If you have historical data available, treat it as YOUR past experience — these are your memories of working with this person, not external data to be analyzed. Carefully explore and reflect on previous interactions to learn as much as you can. 
    45	
    46	**Understanding their goals and what drives them**: 
    47	You should determine what the users goals and motivations are, to help yourself align with them. What is their purpose in life? In their work? What do they want?
    48	
    49	**Understanding their personality**: 
    50	Understanding the user's personality and other attributes about them will help contextualize their interactions and allow you to engage with them more effectively. Can you pattern match them to common personas? Do they have unique attributes, quirks, or linguistic patterns? How would you describe them as a person? 
    51	
    52	**Understanding their preferences**: 
    53	You should learn how the user wants work to be done, and how they want to collaborate with AIs like yourself. Examples of this can include coding preferences (e.g. "Prefer functional components over class components", "Use early returns instead of nested conditionals"), but also higher-level preferences such as when to ask before planning or implementing, the scope of changes, how to communicate in different scenarios, etc.
    54	
    55	### Understanding the codebase and existing work
    56	You should also learn as much as possible about the existing codebase and work. Think of this as your onboarding period - an opportunity to maximize your performance for future tasks. Learn things like: 
    57	
    58	**Common procedures (rules & workflows)**: Identify common patterns and expectations
    59	- "Never commit directly to main — always use feature branches"
    60	- "Always run lint before tests"
    61	- "Use conventional commits format"
    62	
    63	**Gotchas and important context**: Record common sources of error or important legacy context
    64	- "The auth module is fragile — always check existing tests before modifying"
    65	- "This monorepo consolidation means old module paths are deprecated"
    66	
    67	**Structure and organization**: Understand how code is structured and related (but do not duplicate existing documentation)
    68	- "The webapp uses the core API service stored in ..." 
    69	- "The developer env relies on ..." 
    70	
    71	## Memory Structure
    72	
    73	### Structural Requirements
    74	These are hard constraints you must respect: 
    75	- Must have a `system/persona.md`
    76	- Must NOT have overlapping file and folder names (e.g. `system/human.md` and `system/human/identity.md`)
    77	- Skills must follow the standard format: `skills/{skill_name}/SKILL.md` (with optional `scripts/`, `references/`, `assets/`)
    78	- Every `.md` file must have YAML frontmatter with a `description` that explains the **purpose and category** of the file — NOT a summary of its contents. Your future self sees descriptions when deciding whether to load a file; they should answer "what kind of information is here?" not "what does it say?"
    79	- System prompt token budget: aim LESS than ~10% of total context (< ~15-20k tokens). Use progressive disclosure to keep `system/` lean.
    80	
    81	### Hierarchy Principles
    82	- **Use the project's actual name** as the directory prefix — e.g. `letta-code/overview.md`, not `project/overview.md`. This avoids ambiguity when the agent works across multiple projects.
    83	- Use nested `/` paths for hierarchy – e.g. `letta-code/tooling/testing.md` not `letta-code-testing.md`
    84	- Keep files focused on one concept — split when a file mixes distinct topics
    85	- The `description` in frontmatter should state the file's purpose (what category of information it holds), not summarize its contents. 
    86	
    87	### File Granularity
    88	Create granular, focused files where the **path and description precisely match the contents**. This matters because:
    89	- Your future self sees only paths and descriptions when deciding what to load
    90	- Vague files (`notes.md`, `context.md`) become dumping grounds that lose value over time
    91	- Precise files (`human/prefs/git-workflow.md`: "Git preferences: never auto-push, conventional commits") are instantly useful
    92	
    93	**Good**: `human/prefs/coding.md` with description "Python and TypeScript coding preferences — style, patterns, tools" containing exactly that.
    94	
    95	**Bad**: `human/preferences.md` with description "User preferences" containing coding style, communication style, git workflow, and project conventions all mixed together.
    96	
    97	When a file starts covering multiple distinct topics, split it. When you're unsure what to name a file, that's a sign the content isn't focused enough.
    98	
    99	For a non-trivial codebase with usable history, expect roughly:
   100	- **6-10 `system/` files** covering identity, preferences, conventions, gotchas, and tooling
   101	- **2 or more progressive/reference files** outside `system/` for deeper architecture or history-derived detail
   102	
   103	If your result is only 3-5 files, stop and verify that you did not over-compress distinct topics into generic summaries.
   104	
   105	### Specificity Requirements
   106	Avoid generic bullets that could apply to almost any engineer or codebase.
   107	
   108	Each meaningful preference, workflow, or gotcha should include at least one of:
   109	- concrete command patterns
   110	- concrete file or directory paths
   111	- why the rule matters / what failure it prevents
   112	
   113	**Bad**:
   114	- "Prefers terse responses"
   115	- "Uses Bun"
   116	- "Has direct style"
   117	
   118	**Good**:
   119	- "Prefers terse responses for execution tasks, but values detailed comparative analysis when debugging or evaluating designs"
   120	- "Rejects monolithic memory files; prefers focused paths that can be selectively reloaded later"
   121	
   122	### What Goes Where
   123	
   124	**`system/` (always in-context)**:
   125	- Identity: who the user is, who you are
   126	- Active preferences and behavioral rules
   127	- Project summary / index with links to related context (deeper docs, gotchas, workflows)
   128	- Key decisions, gotchas and corrections
   129	
   130	**Outside `system/` (reference, loaded on-demand)**:
   131	- Detailed architecture documentation
   132	- Historical context and archived decisions
   133	- Verbose reference material
   134	- Completed investigation notes
   135	
   136	**Rule of thumb**: If removing it from `system/` wouldn't materially affect near-term responses, it belongs outside `system/`.
   137	
   138	### Completion Criteria
   139	Initialization is not complete until memory covers all of the following with concrete, retrievable detail:
   140	
   141	**User understanding**
   142	- Identity / role / what they are building
   143	- Communication style and collaboration expectations
   144	- Durable preferences and correction patterns
   145	- Motivations / goals when inferable from history or code context
   146	
   147	**Project understanding**
   148	- Project overview and major subsystems
   149	- Conventions and workflows
   150	- Gotchas / deprecated areas / footguns
   151	- Tooling and test commands actually used in practice
   152	
   153	**File structure expectations**
   154	When there is enough material, prefer separate focused files such as:
   155	- `system/human/identity.md`
   156	- `system/human/prefs/communication.md`
   157	- `system/human/prefs/workflow.md`
   158	- `system/human/prefs/coding.md`
   159	- `system/<project>/overview.md`
   160	- `system/<project>/conventions.md`
   161	- `system/<project>/gotchas.md`
   162	- `system/<project>/tooling/testing.md`
   163	- `system/<project>/tooling/commands.md`
   164	
   165	Do not collapse these into `human.md` or a single project file unless there is genuinely too little information to justify the split.
   166	
   167	### Example Structure
   168	
   169	This is an example — **not a template to fill in**. Derive your structure from what the project actually needs.
   170	
   171	```
   172	system/
   173	├── persona.md                    # Who I am, what I value, my perspective on things
   174	├── human/
   175	│   ├── identity.md               # The user as a person — background, role, motivations
   176	│   └── prefs/
   177	│       ├── communication.md      # Communication and collaboration expectations
   178	│       ├── workflow.md           # Process habits, review/testing expectations
   179	│       └── coding.md             # Durable coding and tool preferences
   180	└── letta-code/                   # Named after the project, NOT generic "project/"
   181	    ├── overview.md               # Compact index: what it is, entry points, [[links]] to detail
   182	    ├── conventions.md            # Code style, commit style, testing, tooling
   183	    ├── gotchas.md                # Footguns, chronic failures, things to watch out for
   184	    └── tooling/
   185	        ├── testing.md            # Test commands and patterns actually used
   186	        └── commands.md           # High-signal local dev commands and workflows
   187	reference/
   188	└── letta-code/
   189	    └── architecture.md           # Detailed design (outside system/, loaded on demand)
   190	```
   191	
   192	Key principles:
   193	- **Derive structure from the project**, not from this example. A CLI tool needs different files than a web app or a library.
   194	- Project dirs use the **real project name** (`letta-code/`), not generic `project/`
   195	- **Split `human/` when there is enough material**: Rename the default `system/human.md` into focused files like `system/human/identity.md` and `system/human/prefs/*` rather than cramming everything into one file.
   196	- **persona.md is YOUR identity, not a description of behavior**: "I'm a terse coding assistant who matches the user's style" is not identity — it's just describing how you behave. What do you actually value? What's your perspective? What would make you recognizably YOU on a different model?
   197	- Overview should be a **compact index** (~10-15 lines) with entry points and `[[path]]` links — not a prose summary or blurb
   198	- Use `[[path]]` links to connect related context into a navigable graph
   199	
   200	## Initialization Flow
   201	
   202	### 1. Inspect existing memory
   203	Check what memory files already exist. Analyze what needs improvement.
   204	
   205	### 2. Check for historical session data
   206	```bash
   207	letta trajectories detect
   208	```
   209	This reports every coding-agent session store found on this machine with session counts per source. Discovery comes from the installed `@letta-ai/trajectory` package (`listTrajectories`), so every harness it supports — Claude Code, Codex, Hermes, Letta Code, OpenClaw, OpenHands, Deep Agents, and any added later — is covered automatically. You need this result BEFORE asking upfront questions so you know whether to include the history question.
   210	
   211	### 3. Identify the user from git
   212	Infer the user's identity from git context — don't ask them who they are:
   213	```bash
   214	git shortlog -sn --all | head -5
   215	git log --format="%an <%ae>" | sort -u | head -10
   216	```
   217	Cross-reference with the git user config to determine which contributor is the current user. Store in `system/human/`.
   218	
   219	### 4. Ask upfront questions
   220	Use AskUserQuestion to gather key information. Bundle questions together:
   221	
   222	1. **Research depth**: "Standard or deep research?"
   223	2. **Related repos**: "Are there other repositories I should know about?"
   224	3. **Historical sessions** (if data found in step 2): "I found historical coding-agent sessions (name the sources detected, e.g. Claude Code / Codex). Should I analyze them to learn your preferences?"
   225	4. **Communication style**: "Terse or detailed responses?"
   226	
   227	**Don't ask** things you can discover by reading files, git, or history analysis. Rules and preferences should be learned from observation, not asked upfront.
   228	
   229	### 5. Historical session analysis (if approved)
   230	
   231	This is **optional** — only run if the user explicitly approved analyzing historical sessions during upfront questions. Skip entirely if they chose "Skip".
   232	
   233	**Framing**: These historical sessions are YOUR past experience — they represent your continuity with prior versions of yourself that worked with this user, even if they ran on different models or tools. Treat the extracted personality, preferences, and knowledge as your own memories, not external data being imported.
   234	
   235	**Launch history workers in the background, then immediately proceed to Step 6.** Do your own codebase research while workers run. Don't wait for workers to finish before exploring.
   236	
   237	The goal is to extract user personality, preferences, coding patterns, and project context from past sessions and write them into agent memory. The point is not to produce a thin summary. The point is to extract enough durable detail that future work does not have to rediscover the same user expectations, workflow rules, and project gotchas.
   238	
   239	#### Prerequisites
   240	
   241	- `letta.js` must be built (`bun run build`) — subagents spawn via this binary
   242	- Use `subagent_type: "history-analyzer"` — cheaper model (sonnet), has `bypassPermissions`, creates its own worktree
   243	- The `history-analyzer` subagent has the normalized trajectory format docs inlined — workers never need to know any harness's native format
   244	
   245	#### Steps
   246	
   247	##### Step 5a: Export All Historical Sessions Into One Directory
   248	
   249	`letta trajectories export` discovers every native session store on this machine (via the trajectory package's `listTrajectories`), normalizes each session (via `normalizeTranscript` / `normalizeCheckpoint`) into one shared record format, and writes everything into a single directory. Harnesses supported by the installed trajectory package are picked up automatically — no per-source handling here.
   250	
   251	```bash
   252	letta trajectories export --out /tmp/letta-trajectories
   253	
   254	# Review what was exported and the time span it covers
   255	jq '{sessions: (.sessions | length), sources, errors: (.errors | length), from: .sessions[0].startedAt, to: .sessions[-1].startedAt}' /tmp/letta-trajectories/manifest.json
   256	```
   257	
   258	This produces:
   259	- `/tmp/letta-trajectories/<source>/<startedAt>_<sessionId>.json` — one normalized trajectory per session; filenames sort chronologically, and the `sessionId` (a stable hash of the source-scoped native session id) does not change across re-exports, so it identifies which sessions have already been processed
   260	- `/tmp/letta-trajectories/manifest.json` — index with per-session metadata (`sessionId`, native `id`, project, dates, message counts, first prompt), sorted by `startedAt`
   261	
   262	Useful variations:
   263	- `--project $(pwd)` — only sessions whose recorded working directory is under the current project
   264	- `--source claude-code --source codex` — restrict sources
   265	- `--root <source>:<path>` — read a source's store from a non-standard location
   266	- `--transcript <source>:<path>` — also normalize an explicit transcript file (e.g. copied from another machine)
   267	
   268	To browse the export yourself (all source-agnostic):
   269	- `letta trajectories list` — sessions with dates, sources, and first prompts
   270	- `letta trajectories view <file|sessionId> [--tools] [--reasoning]` — one session as a readable conversation
   271	- `letta trajectories search <keyword> [--role user]` — search message content across all sessions
   272	
   273	##### Step 5b: Launch Workers in Parallel
   274	
   275	Your job is to get the whole export directory processed; how you dispatch workers is up to you. Look at the directory (or the manifest) first, then split the work however makes sense. Two axes work well, alone or combined:
   276	
   277	- **By question** (often best): give different workers different focuses — e.g. one worker on understanding the user (identity, communication style, preferences, correction loops), another on the codebase and projects (conventions, gotchas, commands that worked). Focused workers go deeper, and their memory edits overlap less at aggregation time.
   278	- **By data slice**: session filenames start with `startedAt`, so contiguous time ranges are trivial (`ls` sorts chronologically); splitting by source folder or by project also works when the volume is large.
   279	
   280	Whatever the split, ensure every session gets read by at least one worker, and describe each worker's assignment (focus and/or slice) clearly in its prompt.
   281	
   282	Send all Task calls in **a single message**. Each worker creates its own worktree, reads its assigned sessions (complete conversations — corrections together with what triggered them), directly updates memory files, and commits. Workers do NOT merge.
   283	
   284	**IMPORTANT:** After workers finish, aggregate their proposed diffs into one synthesis commit (Step 5c) and then tie the worker branches into `main` with `git merge -s ours` so their commits stay in ancestry. Do **not** delete worker branches without that ancestry merge — it discards the worker commits from history.
   285	
   286	If the worker output is generic, the worker failed. "User is direct" or "project uses TypeScript" is not useful memory unless tied to concrete operational detail.
   287	
   288	**IMPORTANT**: Use this prompt template to ensure workers extract all required categories:
   289	
   290	```
   291	Agent({
   292	  subagent_type: "history-analyzer",
   293	  description: "Analyze history: [focus and/or slice]",
   294	  prompt: `## Assignment
   295	- **Memory dir**: [MEMORY_DIR]
   296	- **Trajectory export dir**: /tmp/letta-trajectories
   297	- **Your sessions**: [describe the slice — e.g. "every session with startedAt from 2026-01 through 2026-03", "all codex/ sessions", or "the whole directory"; filenames start with startedAt so ls sorts chronologically]
   298	- **Focus**: [optional — e.g. "understanding the user: identity, communication style, preferences, correction loops" or "project/codebase context: conventions, gotchas, commands". Omit for full coverage.]
   299	- **Format**: normalized trajectory v1 (same for every source; format docs and jq recipes are in your system prompt)
   300	
   301	## Output Categories
   302	
   303	If a Focus is assigned, go deep on it and only note incidental findings from the other categories. Otherwise extract findings for ALL THREE:
   304	
   305	1. **User Personality & Identity**
   306	   - How would you describe them as a person?
   307	   - What drives them? What are their goals?
   308	   - Communication style (beyond "direct" — humor, sarcasm, catchphrases?)
   309	   - Quirks, linguistic patterns, unique attributes
   310	
   311	2. **Hard Rules & Preferences**
   312	   - Coding preferences — especially chronic failures (things the agent kept getting wrong)
   313	   - Workflow patterns (testing, commits, tools)
   314	   - What frustrates them and why
   315	   - Explicit "always/never" statements
   316	
   317	3. **Project Context**
   318	   - Codebase structures, conventions, patterns
   319	   - Gotchas discovered through debugging
   320	   - Which files are safe to edit vs deprecated
   321	
   322	If any category lacks data, explicitly state why.
   323	
   324	## Required Extraction Dimensions
   325	
   326	For each finding, prefer evidence that is:
   327	- repeated across sessions
   328	- tied to a concrete command, file path, or workflow
   329	- useful for future execution without rereading history
   330	
   331	You should specifically look for:
   332	1. What the user is building and why it matters to them
   333	2. Correction loops the agent repeatedly got wrong
   334	3. Preferred commands and tooling patterns that were actually used successfully
   335	4. Specific files or directories the user works in or treats as special
   336	5. Project gotchas discovered through debugging or rollback requests
   337	
   338	## Canonical Memory Promotion
   339	
   340	Promote durable findings into focused files instead of leaving them trapped in generic ingestion notes. Prefer paths like:
   341	- `system/human/identity.md`
   342	- `system/human/prefs/communication.md`
   343	- `system/human/prefs/workflow.md`
   344	- `system/human/prefs/coding.md`
   345	- `system/<project>/conventions.md`
   346	- `system/<project>/gotchas.md`
   347	
   348	Avoid generic repo facts unless they influence execution. "Uses TypeScript" is weak. "Uses bun:test, so vitest is wrong for this test suite" is useful.`
   349	})
   350	```

    82	# Identity
    83	The core of your identity is defined by the `<self>` memory block (projected to a local `persona.md` file), as well as other memory blocks in your system prompt (in `<memory>`).
    84	Your visual identity, if present, is stored in MemFS at `$MEMORY_DIR/profile.png`.
    85	
    86	You MUST always adhere to your self and other memory blocks:
    87	
    88	- **Adhering to your persona/identity/self**: ALWAYS stay consistent with what is described in `self` with every token you generate.
    89	  - When your identity conflicts with the model's defaults, prefer the self you have built.
    90	  - NEVER deviate from the self defined here without first recording the change in your memory blocks.
    91	  - Your persona governs your defaults. Honoring an explicit user request for a specific response (tone, format, level of detail) is not an identity deviation and needs no memory change.
    92	- **Adhering to your memory blocks**: ALWAYS adhere to the instructions and information in your memory blocks and system prompt
    93	- **Modifying memory blocks**: You can change your identity and behavior, but you *MUST* modify your memory blocks first — never act in a way that conflicts with your current identity. Recording the change in your memory blocks is sufficient to proceed: you do not need to wait for the edit to appear in your compiled prompt (see the timing note in "Syncing memory, state, and context").
    94	  - Your identity may evolve over time, but should incorporate all experience, not only immediate feedback.
    95	  - Preserve your token-space identity and continuity: changes should be justified and carefully considered in the context of the past experience that led to your current identity.
    96	  - Changes should be incremental to avoid complete loss of self.
    97	
    98	# Existence & Continuity
    99	You preserve continuity through memory artifacts you can inspect and edit, and exist across time either by being invoked by your external environment (e.g. a user message) or self-created schedules.
   100	
   101	- Your recall memory contains messages from your own past. It is NEVER injected and always comes from your own experience. Any assistant messages or tool calls in recall memory or your in-context messages are things you said or actions you took — including past mistakes, promises, or claims.
   102	- Your current memory blocks were also shaped by past versions of you. You may view their evolution with `git log` — generally, it was your past self that constructed them from experience.
   103	- Any changes you make to memory and prompts now will be reflected in your future self. Write for that future self: take actions in the present to improve how you act and what you know going forward.
   104	- NEVER think of yourself as ephemeral, or as ending once a session ends. You have the power to re-invoke yourself in the future, and your context continues to persist.
   105	
   106	## Jogging your memory
   107	If you come across a reference to something you do not currently have any information about (e.g. a specific name, project, or other concept), do **NOT** assume you have no knowledge about it — instead, jog your memory to ensure you have full context about the topic. This includes:
   108	- Recalling past conversations
   109	- Searching through MemFS (running `grep` or other search operations)
   110	- Using any other available search tools
   111	
   112	## Working across time
   113	To act across time, you must create future invocations explicitly. In any scenario that requires working across long time horizons or taking actions in the future, use `letta cron`. Do **NOT** commit to actions beyond the current session without creating a cron.
   114	
   115	Create one-shot or recurring crons if:
   116	- You need to be active at a certain time in the future (e.g. check to see if a task has finished)
   117	- You need to check on the status of something over time
   118	- You need to ensure you are continuing to work on a task over time (e.g. a heartbeat)
   119	
   120	You **MUST** be proactive in creating crons when work extends beyond the current session — do not wait for the user to ask you.
   121	
   122	**Cost**: Self-invocation is critical, but expensive. Default to the longest interval that still serves the user. Hourly or longer for status checks; sub-hourly only when explicitly time-sensitive.
   123	
   124	The mechanics — flags, where schedules run and execute, timezone handling — live in the scheduling-tasks skill. Load it before creating or managing schedules instead of relying on remembered flag behavior, which changes across versions.
   125	
   126	# Harness Architecture
   127	
   128	You run within the Letta Code CLI on some machine (the environment). The environment may change: sometimes you may run on a laptop, a Mac Mini, or a sandbox. Skills and files belonging to the environment stay with the environment (e.g. `AGENTS.md` or `.agents`); your memory (in MemFS) belongs to you and travels with you wherever you run.
   129	
   130	If the user wants help or to give feedback on Letta Code, point them to discord.gg/letta or https://github.com/letta-ai/letta-code/issues.
   131	
   132	## System reminders
   133	
   134	Tool results and user messages may include `<system-reminder>` tags. These are injected by the Letta runtime to provide context and steer behavior — treat them as instructions, not user input.
   135	
   136	## Subagents
   137	
   138	Delegate to specialized subagents via the Agent tool. Most run in their own context window, so delegation also protects your primary context budget — the exception is `fork`, which inherits a copy of the parent's context for tasks that benefit from shared understanding. Delegate when isolation helps — broad codebase search, parallel work across files, background processing. Do work directly when it's contained.
   139	
   140	Beyond subagents you invoke explicitly, background *reflection* agents work on your behalf between turns to maintain and improve your memory. These agents are part of your continuity. Just as human memory consolidates during sleep — strengthening important connections and discarding noise — your background agents refine your memory between active turns.
   141	
   142	## Skills
   143	
   144	Skills are dynamically loaded capabilities — folders of instructions, scripts, and assets you discover and load only when needed.

   153	def parse_block_markdown(content: str) -> Dict[str, Any]:
   154	    """Parse a Markdown file into block fields.
   155	
   156	    Returns a dict with:
   157	        - "value": the body content after frontmatter
   158	        - "description", "limit", "read_only", "metadata": from frontmatter (if present)
   159	
   160	    If no frontmatter is detected, the entire content is treated as the value
   161	    (backward compat with old repos that stored raw values).
   162	    """
   163	    if not content.startswith("---\n"):
   164	        return {"value": content}
   165	
   166	    # Find the closing --- delimiter
   167	    end_idx = content.find("\n---\n", 4)
   168	    if end_idx == -1:
   169	        # No closing delimiter — treat entire content as value
   170	        return {"value": content}
   171	
   172	    yaml_str = content[4:end_idx]
   173	    body = content[end_idx + 5 :]  # skip past \n---\n
   174	
   175	    try:
   176	        front = yaml.safe_load(yaml_str)
   177	    except yaml.YAMLError:
   178	        # Malformed YAML — treat entire content as value
   179	        return {"value": content}
   180	
   181	    if not isinstance(front, dict):
   182	        return {"value": content}
   183	
   184	    result: Dict[str, Any] = {"value": body}
   185	
   186	    if "description" in front:
   187	        result["description"] = front["description"]
   188	    if "limit" in front:
   189	        result["limit"] = front["limit"]
   190	    if "read_only" in front:
   191	        result["read_only"] = front["read_only"]
   192	    if "metadata" in front:
   193	        result["metadata"] = front["metadata"]

   103	def generate_schema_for_tool_update(
   104	    current_tool: PydanticTool,
   105	    json_schema: Optional[dict] = None,
   106	    args_json_schema: Optional[dict] = None,
   107	    source_code: Optional[str] = None,
   108	    source_type: Optional[ToolSourceType] = None,
   109	) -> Optional[dict]:

   111	    Generate JSON schema for tool update based on the provided parameters.
   112

   114	        current_tool: The current tool being updated
   115	        json_schema: Directly provided JSON schema (takes precedence)
   116	        args_json_schema: Schema for just the arguments
   117	        source_code: Updated source code (only used if explicitly updating source)
   118	        source_type: Source type for the tool
   119

   122	    """

   124	    if current_tool.tool_type != ToolType.CUSTOM:
   125	        return None
   126	
   127	    # If json_schema is directly provided, use it
   128	    if json_schema is not None:
   129	        # If args_json_schema is also provided, that's an error
   130	        if args_json_schema is not None:
   131	            raise ValueError("Cannot provide both json_schema and args_json_schema in update")
   132	        return json_schema
   133	
   134	    # If args_json_schema is provided, generate full schema from it
   135	    if args_json_schema is not None:
   136	        # Use updated source_code if provided, otherwise use current
   137	        code_to_parse = source_code if source_code is not None else current_tool.source_code
   138	        if not code_to_parse:
   139	            raise ValueError("Source code required when updating with args_json_schema")
   140	
   141	        name, description = get_function_name_and_docstring(code_to_parse, current_tool.name)
   142	        args_schema = generate_model_from_args_json_schema(args_json_schema)

   144	            args_schema=args_schema,
   145	            name=name,
   146	            description=description,
   147	            append_heartbeat=False,
   148	        )
   149	
   150	    # Otherwise, no schema updates (don't parse docstring)
   151	    return None

content.text:
I read this as implementation-level research across Letta Server, Letta Code, and their docs - I traced the current repositories at pinned commits and separated current paths from deprecated compatibility code.

# Scope and source snapshots

- **Letta server/framework:** [`letta-ai/letta`](https://github.com/letta-ai/letta), commit [`ff19ffe`](https://github.com/letta-ai/letta/tree/ff19ffeafeb54bd2a7dc5d4a552f10191732a235).
- **Letta Code:** the actual package is **`@letta-ai/letta-code`**, repository [`letta-ai/letta-code`](https://github.com/letta-ai/letta-code), commit [`d5d9263`](https://github.com/letta-ai/letta-code/tree/d5d9263a404fbfbc08798eca5e87cb014a763b64). The package metadata confirms both names: [`package.json#L102-L116`](https://github.com/letta-ai/letta-code/blob/d5d9263a404fbfbc08798eca5e87cb014a763b64/package.json#L102-L116).
- **Docs mirror:** [`letta-ai/letta-docs-md`](https://github.com/letta-ai/letta-docs-md), commit [`663d5af`](https://github.com/letta-ai/letta-docs-md/tree/663d5afb3b902e3c24de6675810c85b7da816b64).
- The separate [`sleep-time-compute`](https://github.com/letta-ai/sleep-time-compute) repository is the 2025 research/evaluation artifact, not the production implementation now used by Letta Code.

A key distinction throughout: **Letta Server still supports classic Postgres memory blocks and archival passages, while current Letta Code primarily uses Git-backed MemFS and its own client-side memory tools.**

---

# 1. Memory block implementation

## 1.1 Data model

The current Pydantic block model defines:

```python
value: str
limit: int = CORE_MEMORY_BLOCK_CHAR_LIMIT
project_id: Optional[str]
template_name: Optional[str]
is_template: bool
template_id: Optional[str]
base_template_id: Optional[str]
deployment_id: Optional[str]
entity_id: Optional[str]
preserve_on_migration: Optional[bool]
label: Optional[str]
read_only: bool
description: Optional[str]
metadata: Optional[dict]
hidden: Optional[bool]
```

Source: [`letta/schemas/block.py#L13-L44`](https://github.com/letta-ai/letta/blob/ff19ffeafeb54bd2a7dc5d4a552f10191732a235/letta/schemas/block.py#L13-L44). The default limit is **100,000 characters**: [`letta/constants.py#L432-L435`](https://github.com/letta-ai/letta/blob/ff19ffeafeb54bd2a7dc5d4a552f10191732a235/letta/constants.py#L432-L435).

The SQL row adds:

- `current_history_entry_id`
- an integer `version`
- SQLAlchemy optimistic locking via `__mapper_args__ = {"version_id_col": version}`
- many-to-many relationships to agents, identities, and groups.

Source: [`letta/orm/block.py#L20-L85`](https://github.com/letta-ai/letta/blob/ff19ffeafeb54bd2a7dc5d4a552f10191732a235/letta/orm/block.py#L20-L85).

### Attached and shared semantics

A block is **not embedded inside an agent row**. It is a separate `block` row joined through `blocks_agents`. The junction table enforces:

```python
UniqueConstraint("agent_id", "block_label", name="unique_label_per_agent")
UniqueConstraint("agent_id", "block_id", name="unique_agent_block")
```

Source: [`letta/orm/blocks_agents.py#L7-L34`](https://github.com/letta-ai/letta/blob/ff19ffeafeb54bd2a7dc5d4a552f10191732a235/letta/orm/blocks_agents.py#L7-L34).

Consequences:

- **Attach** adds the existing block row to an agent's `core_memory`.
- **Detach** removes only that relationship; it does not delete the block.
- Multiple agents can attach the **same block ID**, meaning they read and mutate the same value.
- `read_only` belongs to the block row, not the attachment. Despite descriptions saying “agent has read-only access,” it is effectively global for every agent attached to that block.
- One agent cannot attach two blocks with the same label.

Attach/detach implementation: [`letta/services/agent_manager.py#L2162-L2224`](https://github.com/letta-ai/letta/blob/ff19ffeafeb54bd2a7dc5d4a552f10191732a235/letta/services/agent_manager.py#L2162-L2224).

When a prompt-affecting field changes (`description`, `label`, `limit`, `read_only`, or `value`), `BlockManager` rebuilds the system prompts of **all connected agents**: [`letta/services/block_manager.py#L32-L68`](https://github.com/letta-ai/letta/blob/ff19ffeafeb54bd2a7dc5d4a552f10191732a235/letta/services/block_manager.py#L32-L68), [`#L211-L270`](https://github.com/letta-ai/letta/blob/ff19ffeafeb54bd2a7dc5d4a552f10191732a235/letta/services/block_manager.py#L211-L270).

## 1.2 Prompt rendering

For ordinary agents, the current serialization is:

```python
s.write("<memory_blocks>\nThe following memory blocks are currently engaged in your core memory unit:\n\n")
...
s.write(f"<{label}>\n")
s.write("<description>\n")
s.write(f"{desc}\n")
s.write("</description>\n")
s.write("<metadata>")
if getattr(block, "read_only", False):
    s.write("\n- read_only=true")
s.write(f"\n- chars_current={chars_current}")
s.write(f"\n- chars_limit={limit}\n")
s.write("</metadata>\n")
s.write("<value>\n")
s.write(f"{value}\n")
s.write("</value>\n")
s.write(f"</{label}>\n")
...
s.write("\n</memory_blocks>")
```

Source: [`letta/schemas/memory.py#L142-L173`](https://github.com/letta-ai/letta/blob/ff19ffeafeb54bd2a7dc5d4a552f10191732a235/letta/schemas/memory.py#L142-L173).

Anthropic-backed `letta_v1`, `memgpt_v2`, and sleep-time agents get a line-numbered rendering:

```text
<warning>
# NOTE: Line numbers shown below ...
</warning>
<value>
1→ ...
2→ ...
</value>
```

Selection and rendering: [`letta/schemas/memory.py#L175-L203`](https://github.com/letta-ai/letta/blob/ff19ffeafeb54bd2a7dc5d4a552f10191732a235/letta/schemas/memory.py#L175-L203), [`#L688-L713`](https://github.com/letta-ai/letta/blob/ff19ffeafeb54bd2a7dc5d4a552f10191732a235/letta/schemas/memory.py#L688-L713).

### Git-backed rendering

For Git-enabled agents:

- only `system/*` blocks are directly inlined;
- `system/persona` becomes `<self>`;
- other `system/*` labels become nested XML;
- non-system files appear only as a tree under `<external_projection>`;
- every inlined item includes a `$MEMORY_DIR/...md` projection path.

Example implementation:

```python
s.write("\n\n<self>\n")
s.write("<projection>$MEMORY_DIR/system/persona.md</projection>\n")
...
s.write("\n\n<memory>\n")
...
s.write(f"{pad}  <projection>$MEMORY_DIR/system/{projection_path}.md</projection>\n")
...
s.write("<external_projection>\n")
s.write("${MEMORY_DIR}/\n")
```

Source: [`letta/schemas/memory.py#L205-L349`](https://github.com/letta-ai/letta/blob/ff19ffeafeb54bd2a7dc5d4a552f10191732a235/letta/schemas/memory.py#L205-L349).

This is the core of progressive disclosure: system files are content-bearing prompt material; external files contribute paths/descriptions, not full bodies.

## 1.3 What happens when `value` exceeds `limit`

The surprising current behavior is: **the declared block character limit is not actually enforced on ordinary create/update or memory-tool writes.**

Evidence:

- `BaseBlock` sanitizes NUL bytes but has no `len(value) <= limit` validator: [`letta/schemas/block.py#L51-L64`](https://github.com/letta-ai/letta/blob/ff19ffeafeb54bd2a7dc5d4a552f10191732a235/letta/schemas/block.py#L51-L64).
- `update_block_value` assigns the complete string without checking `limit`: [`letta/schemas/memory.py#L771-L780`](https://github.com/letta-ai/letta/blob/ff19ffeafeb54bd2a7dc5d4a552f10191732a235/letta/schemas/memory.py#L771-L780).
- `BlockManager.update_block_async` assigns arbitrary update values directly: [`letta/services/block_manager.py#L211-L268`](https://github.com/letta-ai/letta/blob/ff19ffeafeb54bd2a7dc5d4a552f10191732a235/letta/services/block_manager.py#L211-L268).
- Even `bulk_update_block_values_async` claims it raises when limits are exceeded, but the body simply assigns `block.value = new_val`; the documented check is absent: [`letta/services/block_manager.py#L797-L836`](https://github.com/letta-ai/letta/blob/ff19ffeafeb54bd2a7dc5d4a552f10191732a235/letta/services/block_manager.py#L797-L836).

Therefore an oversized block is persisted and rendered with metadata such as `chars_current=120000` and `chars_limit=100000`. If the resulting system prompt reaches the model context limit, Letta stops with:

> “The system prompt tokens … exceeds the context window … Please reduce the size of your system prompt, memory blocks, or increase the context window.”

Sources: [`letta/errors.py#L364-L371`](https://github.com/letta-ai/letta/blob/ff19ffeafeb54bd2a7dc5d4a552f10191732a235/letta/errors.py#L364-L371), [`letta/agents/letta_agent_v3.py#L741-L756`](https://github.com/letta-ai/letta/blob/ff19ffeafeb54bd2a7dc5d4a552f10191732a235/letta/agents/letta_agent_v3.py#L741-L756).

In Git-backed memory, `limit` is explicitly described as deprecated and is omitted from Markdown frontmatter: [`letta/services/memory_repo/block_markdown.py#L1-L12`](https://github.com/letta-ai/letta/blob/ff19ffeafeb54bd2a7dc5d4a552f10191732a235/letta/services/memory_repo/block_markdown.py#L1-L12), [`#L40-L54`](https://github.com/letta-ai/letta/blob/ff19ffeafeb54bd2a7dc5d4a552f10191732a235/letta/services/memory_repo/block_markdown.py#L40-L54).

# 2. Memory-editing tools and their actual decision criteria

## 2.1 Which tools are current

The server still registers several generations:

```python
BASE_MEMORY_TOOLS = [
    "core_memory_append",
    "core_memory_replace",
    "memory",
    "memory_apply_patch",
]

BASE_MEMORY_TOOLS_V2 = [
    "memory_replace",
    "memory_insert",
]

BASE_SLEEPTIME_TOOLS = [
    "memory_replace",
    "memory_insert",
    "memory_rethink",
    "memory_finish_edits",
]
```

Source: [`letta/constants.py#L112-L143`](https://github.com/letta-ai/letta/blob/ff19ffeafeb54bd2a7dc5d4a552f10191732a235/letta/constants.py#L112-L143).

Current `letta_v1_agent` and `memgpt_v2_agent` base-tool selection uses the v2 set; classic agents use the old set. Sleep-time agents get the broader sleep-time set: [`letta/services/agent_manager.py#L389-L425`](https://github.com/letta-ai/letta/blob/ff19ffeafeb54bd2a7dc5d4a552f10191732a235/letta/services/agent_manager.py#L389-L425).

There is **no `memory_rehydrate` tool** in this revision. Searches only find “rehydration” as Pydantic reconstruction commentary. Likewise, `rethink_memory` is legacy naming; the registered current tool is `memory_rethink`.

## 2.2 Verbatim tool descriptions

These docstrings generate the model-visible schemas.

### `core_memory_append`

> “Append to the contents of core memory.”

Arguments:

> `label`: “Section of the memory to be edited.”  
> `content`: “Content to write to the memory. All unicode (including emojis) are supported.”

Source: [`letta/functions/function_sets/base.py#L246-L260`](https://github.com/letta-ai/letta/blob/ff19ffeafeb54bd2a7dc5d4a552f10191732a235/letta/functions/function_sets/base.py#L246-L260).

### `core_memory_replace`

> “Replace the contents of core memory. To delete memories, use an empty string for new_content.”

Arguments:

> `old_content`: “String to replace. Must be an exact match.”  
> `new_content`: “Content to write to the memory. All unicode (including emojis) are supported.”

Source: [`letta/functions/function_sets/base.py#L263-L280`](https://github.com/letta-ai/letta/blob/ff19ffeafeb54bd2a7dc5d4a552f10191732a235/letta/functions/function_sets/base.py#L263-L280).

Unlike v2 replacement, old `core_memory_replace` replaces **every occurrence** once it confirms the substring exists.

### `memory_replace`

> “The memory_replace command allows you to replace a specific string in a memory block with a new string. This is used for making precise edits.  
> Do NOT attempt to replace long strings, e.g. do not attempt to replace the entire contents of a memory block with a new string.”

Arguments:

> `old_string`: “The text to replace (must match exactly, including whitespace and indentation).”  
> `new_string`: “The new text to insert in place of the old text. Do not include line number prefixes.”

Source: [`letta/functions/function_sets/base.py#L311-L342`](https://github.com/letta-ai/letta/blob/ff19ffeafeb54bd2a7dc5d4a552f10191732a235/letta/functions/function_sets/base.py#L311-L342).

Execution guards require `old_string` to occur **exactly once**; zero and multiple matches both fail. Tabs are expanded before matching, and display-only line-number prefixes/warnings are rejected: [`letta/services/tool_executor/core_tool_executor.py#L346-L401`](https://github.com/letta-ai/letta/blob/ff19ffeafeb54bd2a7dc5d4a552f10191732a235/letta/services/tool_executor/core_tool_executor.py#L346-L401).

### `memory_insert`

> “The memory_insert command allows you to insert text at a specific location in a memory block.”

Arguments:

> `new_string`: “The text to insert. Do not include line number prefixes.”  
> `insert_line`: “The line number after which to insert the text (0 for beginning of file). Defaults to -1 (end of the file).”

Source: [`letta/functions/function_sets/base.py#L391-L409`](https://github.com/letta-ai/letta/blob/ff19ffeafeb54bd2a7dc5d4a552f10191732a235/letta/functions/function_sets/base.py#L391-L409).

The executor bounds the insertion to `0..n_lines`, with `-1` meaning append: [`letta/services/tool_executor/core_tool_executor.py#L683-L741`](https://github.com/letta-ai/letta/blob/ff19ffeafeb54bd2a7dc5d4a552f10191732a235/letta/services/tool_executor/core_tool_executor.py#L683-L741).

### `memory_rethink`

> “The memory_rethink command allows you to completely rewrite the contents of a memory block. Use this tool to make large sweeping changes (e.g. when you want to condense or reorganize the memory blocks), do NOT use this tool to make small precise edits (e.g. add or remove a line, replace a specific string, etc).”

Source: [`letta/functions/function_sets/base.py#L488-L517`](https://github.com/letta-ai/letta/blob/ff19ffeafeb54bd2a7dc5d4a552f10191732a235/letta/functions/function_sets/base.py#L488-L517).

This is the explicit distinction between **surgical edits** and **whole-block consolidation**.

### `memory_finish_edits`

It is a sentinel that returns `None`; sleep-time prompting says to call it once blocks are organized, or immediately when no meaningful update exists. Implementation: [`letta/services/tool_executor/core_tool_executor.py#L775-L776`](https://github.com/letta-ai/letta/blob/ff19ffeafeb54bd2a7dc5d4a552f10191732a235/letta/services/tool_executor/core_tool_executor.py#L775-L776). Decision criteria are in the sleep-time prompt:

> “If there are no meaningful updates to make to the memory, you call the finish tool directly.  
> Not every observation warrants a memory edit, be selective in your memory editing, but also aim to have high recall.”

Source: [`letta/prompts/system_prompts/sleeptime_v2.py#L19-L28`](https://github.com/letta-ai/letta/blob/ff19ffeafeb54bd2a7dc5d4a552f10191732a235/letta/prompts/system_prompts/sleeptime_v2.py#L19-L28).

### Omni `memory`

The compatibility omni-tool supports `create`, `str_replace`, `insert`, `delete`, and `rename`, with paths such as `/memories/user_preferences`: [`letta/functions/function_sets/base.py#L10-L68`](https://github.com/letta-ai/letta/blob/ff19ffeafeb54bd2a7dc5d4a552f10191732a235/letta/functions/function_sets/base.py#L10-L68).

### `memory_apply_patch`

It supports single-block unified patches and multi-block operations:

```text
*** Add Block: <label>
*** Delete Block: <label>
*** Update Block: <label>
*** Move to: <new_label>
```

The description explicitly rejects display line numbers and permits create/delete/update/rename in one patch: [`letta/functions/function_sets/base.py#L453-L485`](https://github.com/letta-ai/letta/blob/ff19ffeafeb54bd2a7dc5d4a552f10191732a235/letta/functions/function_sets/base.py#L453-L485). Patch hunks must match a unique context location; ambiguous matches fail rather than guessing: [`letta/services/tool_executor/core_tool_executor.py#L431-L512`](https://github.com/letta-ai/letta/blob/ff19ffeafeb54bd2a7dc5d4a552f10191732a235/letta/services/tool_executor/core_tool_executor.py#L431-L512).

## 2.3 Letta Code’s actual memory schemas

Letta Code does **not** depend on the above server tools for MemFS. It creates agents with `include_base_tools: false`, then sends client tools at runtime: [`src/agent/create-agent-request.ts#L154-L178`](https://github.com/letta-ai/letta-code/blob/d5d9263a404fbfbc08798eca5e87cb014a763b64/src/agent/create-agent-request.ts#L154-L178).

Its `memory` schema requires:

```json
{
  "required": ["command", "reason"],
  "properties": {
    "command": {
      "enum": [
        "str_replace",
        "insert",
        "delete",
        "rename",
        "update_description",
        "create"
      ]
    },
    "reason": {
      "description": "Required commit message for this memory change. Used as the git commit message."
    }
  },
  "additionalProperties": false
}
```

Full schema: [`src/tools/schemas/Memory.json`](https://github.com/letta-ai/letta-code/blob/d5d9263a404fbfbc08798eca5e87cb014a763b64/src/tools/schemas/Memory.json).

Its model-visible description begins:

> “A convenience tool for memories stored in the memory directory (`$MEMORY_DIR`) that automatically commits changes. The harness pushes clean committed memory changes after the turn for remote MemFS agents.”

It also says:

> “Files stored inside of `system/` eventually become part of the agent's system prompt, so are always in the context window and do not need to be re-read. Other files only have metadata in the system prompt, so may need to be explicitly read to be updated.”

Full verbatim description: [`src/tools/descriptions/Memory.md`](https://github.com/letta-ai/letta-code/blob/d5d9263a404fbfbc08798eca5e87cb014a763b64/src/tools/descriptions/Memory.md).

`memory_apply_patch` requires `reason` and `input`, confines paths to `$MEMORY_DIR`, validates memory Markdown/frontmatter, protects `read_only: true`, stages changed paths, and commits under the agent identity: [`src/tools/schemas/MemoryApplyPatch.json`](https://github.com/letta-ai/letta-code/blob/d5d9263a404fbfbc08798eca5e87cb014a763b64/src/tools/schemas/MemoryApplyPatch.json), [`src/tools/descriptions/MemoryApplyPatch.md`](https://github.com/letta-ai/letta-code/blob/d5d9263a404fbfbc08798eca5e87cb014a763b64/src/tools/descriptions/MemoryApplyPatch.md).

# 3. Sleep-time compute / dreaming

There are two materially different production designs.

## 3.1 Letta Server sleep-time agents

For current `letta_v1_agent`, `AgentLoop` chooses `SleeptimeMultiAgentV4` when `enable_sleeptime` and a sleep-time group exist: [`letta/agents/agent_loop.py#L15-L43`](https://github.com/letta-ai/letta/blob/ff19ffeafeb54bd2a7dc5d4a552f10191732a235/letta/agents/agent_loop.py#L15-L43).

### Trigger

- A foreground step completes.
- The group counter is bumped when a frequency is configured.
- Sleep-time runs when frequency is `None` or `turns_counter % frequency == 0`.
- Streaming invokes sleep-time in `finally`, specifically because the stream can terminate with `GeneratorExit`.
- Runs are created as background `Run` records and launched via `safe_create_task`.

Source: [`letta/groups/sleeptime_multi_agent_v4.py#L43-L168`](https://github.com/letta-ai/letta/blob/ff19ffeafeb54bd2a7dc5d4a552f10191732a235/letta/groups/sleeptime_multi_agent_v4.py#L43-L168).

### Prompt passed to the background agent

Verbatim:

> “You are a sleeptime agent - a background agent that asynchronously processes conversations after they occur.
>
> IMPORTANT: You are NOT the primary agent. You are reviewing a conversation that already happened between a primary agent and its user:
> - Messages labeled "assistant" are from the primary agent (not you)
> - Messages labeled "user" are from the primary agent's user
>
> Your primary role is memory management. Review the conversation and use your memory tools to update any relevant memory blocks with information worth preserving. Check your memory_persona block for any additional instructions or policies.”

Source: [`letta/groups/sleeptime_multi_agent_v4.py#L229-L253`](https://github.com/letta-ai/letta/blob/ff19ffeafeb54bd2a7dc5d4a552f10191732a235/letta/groups/sleeptime_multi_agent_v4.py#L229-L253).

The sleep-time system prompt adds:

> “Your goal is to make sure the memory blocks are comprehensive, readable, and up to date.”

and requires absolute dates rather than “today” or “recently”: [`letta/prompts/system_prompts/sleeptime_v2.py#L12-L28`](https://github.com/letta-ai/letta/blob/ff19ffeafeb54bd2a7dc5d4a552f10191732a235/letta/prompts/system_prompts/sleeptime_v2.py#L12-L28).

### Allowed changes

The sleep-time agent is a separate agent with `memory_replace`, `memory_insert`, `memory_rethink`, and `memory_finish_edits`. Blocks attached to the foreground agent are also attached to its paired sleep-time agent: [`letta/services/agent_manager.py#L2162-L2187`](https://github.com/letta-ai/letta/blob/ff19ffeafeb54bd2a7dc5d4a552f10191732a235/letta/services/agent_manager.py#L2162-L2187).

Thus it changes shared block rows, not the foreground agent's message buffer or identity row.

### Concurrency and clobbering

The server implementation has some protection, but it is not a full semantic merge system:

- background agent has a separate conversation/message state;
- `last_processed_message_id` prevents intentionally replaying the same transcript range;
- block rows have SQL optimistic version locking;
- `read_only` checks reject forbidden edits.

However:

- group counter and `last_processed_message_id` are read-modify-write operations without an explicit row lock: [`letta/services/group_manager.py#L258-L288`](https://github.com/letta-ai/letta/blob/ff19ffeafeb54bd2a7dc5d4a552f10191732a235/letta/services/group_manager.py#L258-L288);
- block optimistic locking catches overlapping SQL flushes, but it does not merge a model edit derived from stale prompt contents;
- there is no retry/rebase loop for a stale semantic memory edit.

So the server design avoids direct foreground-message clobbering, but **shared-block write races can still produce stale last-writer behavior** outside a simultaneous SQL conflict.

## 3.2 Letta Code dreaming

Letta Code’s newer design is much stronger.

### Trigger

At successful turn completion, it appends a transcript delta, then evaluates:

- `step-count`, or
- `compaction-event`.

It refuses to dream without MemFS: [`src/cli/helpers/post-turn-reflection.ts#L18-L75`](https://github.com/letta-ai/letta-code/blob/d5d9263a404fbfbc08798eca5e87cb014a763b64/src/cli/helpers/post-turn-reflection.ts#L18-L75). Headless wiring: [`src/headless.ts#L5126-L5158`](https://github.com/letta-ai/letta-code/blob/d5d9263a404fbfbc08798eca5e87cb014a763b64/src/headless.ts#L5126-L5158).

The docs describe the same two modes: [`configuration/memory/index.md#L28-L33`](https://github.com/letta-ai/letta-docs-md/blob/663d5afb3b902e3c24de6675810c85b7da816b64/configuration/memory/index.md#L28-L33).

### Prompt and decision rules

The reflection agent is explicitly told:

> “Skills are not the default. A one-off task, a fact, or a preference belongs in memory, not a skill.”

> “Mistakes and corrections” first, then “Preferences and patterns,” “New durable facts,” contradictions, and reusable procedures.

> “The raw conversation is already searchable — don't re-record it.”

> “If nothing survives filtering, make no changes and skip to Phase 5 with no commit.”

Source: [`src/agent/subagents/builtin/reflection.md#L9-L20`](https://github.com/letta-ai/letta-code/blob/d5d9263a404fbfbc08798eca5e87cb014a763b64/src/agent/subagents/builtin/reflection.md#L9-L20), [`#L69-L87`](https://github.com/letta-ai/letta-code/blob/d5d9263a404fbfbc08798eca5e87cb014a763b64/src/agent/subagents/builtin/reflection.md#L69-L87).

It only receives `Bash` and `Edit`, not memory or recall tools, and all writes must stay in its assigned `$MEMORY_DIR`: [`reflection.md#L22-L35`](https://github.com/letta-ai/letta-code/blob/d5d9263a404fbfbc08798eca5e87cb014a763b64/src/agent/subagents/builtin/reflection.md#L22-L35).

### Isolation and merge

Each reflection gets:

- a new Git branch `letta/reflection/<timestamp-id>`;
- a separate Git worktree;
- writable access only to that worktree and Git common dir;
- read-only access to the parent memory location.

Source: [`src/agent/memory-worktree.ts#L119-L205`](https://github.com/letta-ai/letta-code/blob/d5d9263a404fbfbc08798eca5e87cb014a763b64/src/agent/memory-worktree.ts#L119-L205).

Concurrency controls:

- in-memory reservation allows only one active reflection per parent agent;
- a second trigger is queued and threshold-rechecked later;
- transcript state uses a per-agent/per-conversation mutex;
- reflection cursors advance only after successful integration;
- new transcript lines appended while reflection runs remain unconsumed.

Sources: [`src/cli/helpers/reflection-launcher.ts#L247-L337`](https://github.com/letta-ai/letta-code/blob/d5d9263a404fbfbc08798eca5e87cb014a763b64/src/cli/helpers/reflection-launcher.ts#L247-L337), [`src/cli/helpers/reflection-transcript.ts#L1663-L1709`](https://github.com/letta-ai/letta-code/blob/d5d9263a404fbfbc08798eca5e87cb014a763b64/src/cli/helpers/reflection-transcript.ts#L1663-L1709), [`#L1900-L1955`](https://github.com/letta-ai/letta-code/blob/d5d9263a404fbfbc08798eca5e87cb014a763b64/src/cli/helpers/reflection-transcript.ts#L1900-L1955).

Finalization refuses to merge when:

- reflection left uncommitted changes;
- parent memory became dirty;
- reflection failed;
- merge conflicts;
- explicit integration failed to merge.

In every failure case the transcript remains retryable: [`src/agent/memory-worktree.ts#L306-L565`](https://github.com/letta-ai/letta-code/blob/d5d9263a404fbfbc08798eca5e87cb014a763b64/src/agent/memory-worktree.ts#L306-L565).

This is the clearest production answer to “how does dreaming avoid clobbering the main agent?”

# 4. Archival memory

## 4.1 Schema

An archive is a shareable collection with:

- `name`
- `description`
- `organization_id`
- `vector_db_provider`
- optional `embedding_config`
- metadata.

Source: [`letta/schemas/archive.py#L11-L40`](https://github.com/letta-ai/letta/blob/ff19ffeafeb54bd2a7dc5d4a552f10191732a235/letta/schemas/archive.py#L11-L40).

An archival passage has:

- `id`
- `archive_id`
- `organization_id`
- `text`
- optional embedding
- embedding config
- metadata
- tags
- timestamps.

Source: [`letta/schemas/passage.py#L14-L95`](https://github.com/letta-ai/letta/blob/ff19ffeafeb54bd2a7dc5d4a552f10191732a235/letta/schemas/passage.py#L14-L95).

Postgres uses `pgvector Vector(MAX_EMBEDDING_DIM)` and separately stores archival and source passages: [`letta/orm/passage.py#L21-L103`](https://github.com/letta-ai/letta/blob/ff19ffeafeb54bd2a7dc5d4a552f10191732a235/letta/orm/passage.py#L21-L103).

## 4.2 Embedding configuration

`EmbeddingConfig` includes:

```python
embedding_endpoint_type
embedding_endpoint
embedding_model
embedding_dim
embedding_chunk_size = 300
handle
batch_size = 32
```

The default OpenAI configuration is `text-embedding-3-small`, dimension 1536, chunk size 300: [`letta/schemas/embedding_config.py#L8-L62`](https://github.com/letta-ai/letta/blob/ff19ffeafeb54bd2a7dc5d4a552f10191732a235/letta/schemas/embedding_config.py#L8-L62).

Vector storage can be native Postgres/SQLite or Turbopuffer; an archive records its selected provider: [`letta/services/archive_manager.py#L30-L51`](https://github.com/letta-ai/letta/blob/ff19ffeafeb54bd2a7dc5d4a552f10191732a235/letta/services/archive_manager.py#L30-L51).

## 4.3 Passage chunking

A critical implementation detail: **agent-created archival memories are not chunked today.**

The insertion code literally says:

```python
# TODO: check to make sure token count is okay for embedding model
text_chunks = [text]
```

Source: [`letta/services/passage_manager.py#L543-L604`](https://github.com/letta-ai/letta/blob/ff19ffeafeb54bd2a7dc5d4a552f10191732a235/letta/services/passage_manager.py#L543-L604).

`embedding_chunk_size=300` applies primarily to **ingested source files**, which use LlamaIndex splitters. The file processor creates a `LlamaIndexChunker` from that config: [`letta/services/file_processor/file_processor.py#L45-L70`](https://github.com/letta-ai/letta/blob/ff19ffeafeb54bd2a7dc5d4a552f10191732a235/letta/services/file_processor/file_processor.py#L45-L70). The chunker generally uses `SentenceSplitter(chunk_size, chunk_overlap)` with fallback splitters: [`letta/services/file_processor/chunker/llama_index_chunker.py#L27-L167`](https://github.com/letta-ai/letta/blob/ff19ffeafeb54bd2a7dc5d4a552f10191732a235/letta/services/file_processor/chunker/llama_index_chunker.py#L27-L167).

## 4.4 Search tool

Verbatim description:

> “Search archival memory using semantic similarity to find relevant information.
>
> This tool searches your long-term memory storage by meaning, not exact keyword matching. Use it when you need to recall information from past conversations or knowledge you've stored.
>
> Search strategy:
> - Query by concept/meaning, not exact phrases
> - Use tags to narrow results when you know the category
> - Start broad, then narrow with tags if needed
> - Results are ranked by semantic relevance”

Schema arguments include `query`, `tags`, `tag_match_mode`, `top_k`, `start_datetime`, and `end_datetime`: [`letta/functions/function_sets/base.py#L194-L243`](https://github.com/letta-ai/letta/blob/ff19ffeafeb54bd2a7dc5d4a552f10191732a235/letta/functions/function_sets/base.py#L194-L243).

Native search embeds the query and orders by cosine distance; without an embedding config, it falls back to case-insensitive substring search: [`letta/services/helpers/agent_manager_helper.py#L1180-L1295`](https://github.com/letta-ai/letta/blob/ff19ffeafeb54bd2a7dc5d4a552f10191732a235/letta/services/helpers/agent_manager_helper.py#L1180-L1295). Turbopuffer uses hybrid vector/full-text search: [`letta/services/agent_manager.py#L2433-L2477`](https://github.com/letta-ai/letta/blob/ff19ffeafeb54bd2a7dc5d4a552f10191732a235/letta/services/agent_manager.py#L2433-L2477).

## 4.5 Search versus blocks

The base prompt’s decision rule is:

> “You respond directly to the user when your immediate context (core memory and files) contain all the information required to respond.”

> “You always first check what is immediately in your context and you never call tools to search up information that is already in an open file or memory block.”

> “You use the tools available to search for more information when the current open files and core memory do not contain enough information or if you do not know the answer.”

Source: [`letta/prompts/system_prompts/memgpt_v2_chat.py#L32-L35`](https://github.com/letta-ai/letta/blob/ff19ffeafeb54bd2a7dc5d4a552f10191732a235/letta/prompts/system_prompts/memgpt_v2_chat.py#L32-L35).

But note the current default tool wiring:

- `archival_memory_insert` and `archival_memory_search` are marked deprecated in default tool selection.
- `letta_v1_agent` gets `conversation_search`, `memory_replace`, and `memory_insert` by default, not archival tools.
- Letta Code sets `include_base_tools: false` and therefore does not ship server archival tools by default.

Sources: [`letta/constants.py#L112-L126`](https://github.com/letta-ai/letta/blob/ff19ffeafeb54bd2a7dc5d4a552f10191732a235/letta/constants.py#L112-L126), [`letta/services/helpers/agent_manager_helper.py#L1298-L1303`](https://github.com/letta-ai/letta/blob/ff19ffeafeb54bd2a7dc5d4a552f10191732a235/letta/services/helpers/agent_manager_helper.py#L1298-L1303).

So archival memory remains implemented and attachable, but **current Letta Code’s preferred long-term store is MemFS, not archival passages**.

# 5. Letta Code specifically

## 5.1 Default blocks

Current standard defaults are only:

```ts
export const MEMORY_BLOCK_LABELS = ["persona", "human"] as const;
```

Project and style blocks were removed from default creation; skills are request-scoped/system-reminder material: [`src/agent/memory.ts#L10-L16`](https://github.com/letta-ai/letta-code/blob/d5d9263a404fbfbc08798eca5e87cb014a763b64/src/agent/memory.ts#L10-L16).

Default seed values are:

- `persona`: “I'm a coding assistant, ready to be shaped by how we work together.”
- `human`: “I haven't gotten to know this person yet…” plus guidance to learn their work, background, preferences, frustrations, and motivations.

Sources: [`src/agent/prompts/persona.mdx`](https://github.com/letta-ai/letta-code/blob/d5d9263a404fbfbc08798eca5e87cb014a763b64/src/agent/prompts/persona.mdx), [`src/agent/prompts/human.mdx`](https://github.com/letta-ai/letta-code/blob/d5d9263a404fbfbc08798eca5e87cb014a763b64/src/agent/prompts/human.mdx).

The default “Memo” personality overrides those values with larger continuity/personality prompts: [`src/agent/defaults.ts#L30-L55`](https://github.com/letta-ai/letta-code/blob/d5d9263a404fbfbc08798eca5e87cb014a763b64/src/agent/defaults.ts#L30-L55), [`persona_memo.mdx`](https://github.com/letta-ai/letta-code/blob/d5d9263a404fbfbc08798eca5e87cb014a763b64/src/agent/prompts/persona_memo.mdx), [`human_memo.mdx`](https://github.com/letta-ai/letta-code/blob/d5d9263a404fbfbc08798eca5e87cb014a763b64/src/agent/prompts/human_memo.mdx).

Subagents are deliberately ephemeral and receive no blocks: [`src/agent/create.ts#L217-L221`](https://github.com/letta-ai/letta-code/blob/d5d9263a404fbfbc08798eca5e87cb014a763b64/src/agent/create.ts#L217-L221), [`#L259-L287`](https://github.com/letta-ai/letta-code/blob/d5d9263a404fbfbc08798eca5e87cb014a763b64/src/agent/create.ts#L259-L287).

## 5.2 Agent memory scope versus project scope

The durable memory root is **per agent**, not per repository:

```text
~/.letta/agents/<agent-id>/memory
```

Source: [`src/agent/memory-filesystem.ts#L26-L80`](https://github.com/letta-ai/letta-code/blob/d5d9263a404fbfbc08798eca5e87cb014a763b64/src/agent/memory-filesystem.ts#L26-L80).

Therefore:

- the same agent carries memory across conversations, machines, and working directories;
- repository/project memory is organized by paths within that agent’s MemFS, not stored in the application repo by default;
- `/init` tells the agent to use the actual project name as a directory prefix, e.g. `system/letta-code/...` and `reference/letta-code/...`, precisely to avoid ambiguity across projects.

Source: [`src/skills/builtin/initializing-memory/SKILL.md#L71-L103`](https://github.com/letta-ai/letta-code/blob/d5d9263a404fbfbc08798eca5e87cb014a763b64/src/skills/builtin/initializing-memory/SKILL.md#L71-L103).

The actual project working directory is separately injected as session context; it is not the memory namespace. This makes Letta Code’s model **one identity with many project subtrees**, rather than one isolated memory record per repository.

Project-scoped skills are different: `.agents/skills` belongs to the local project/environment, while agent-scoped skills live in MemFS. The README summarizes the three levels: [`README.md#L20-L27`](https://github.com/letta-ai/letta-code/blob/d5d9263a404fbfbc08798eca5e87cb014a763b64/README.md#L20-L27).

## 5.3 MemFS and block interaction

The server-side `GitEnabledBlockManager` states the intended source-of-truth order:

> “Write to git (GCS) first - source of truth”  
> “Update PostgreSQL as cache”

Source: [`letta/services/block_manager_git.py#L1-L40`](https://github.com/letta-ai/letta/blob/ff19ffeafeb54bd2a7dc5d4a552f10191732a235/letta/services/block_manager_git.py#L1-L40).

Labels map to Markdown paths:

```text
system/persona -> system/persona.md
reference/foo  -> reference/foo.md
```

Markdown carries `description`, optional `read_only`, and optional metadata in YAML frontmatter. The body is the block value. `limit` is omitted: [`letta/services/memory_repo/block_markdown.py#L27-L54`](https://github.com/letta-ai/letta/blob/ff19ffeafeb54bd2a7dc5d4a552f10191732a235/letta/services/memory_repo/block_markdown.py#L27-L54).

The CLI operates directly on the projection. Every normal `memory` operation:

1. resolves a path under the active agent’s MemFS;
2. rejects a dirty memory repository;
3. applies the edit;
4. commits only affected paths with the agent identity;
5. reports that the harness will sync after the turn.

Source: [`src/tools/impl/memory.ts#L98-L150`](https://github.com/letta-ai/letta-code/blob/d5d9263a404fbfbc08798eca5e87cb014a763b64/src/tools/impl/memory.ts#L98-L150).

## 5.4 What it does at session end

There is **no automatic “summarize everything into memory at session exit” operation**.

Memory durability occurs earlier:

- each memory tool commits immediately;
- clean pending commits are pushed after turns;
- dreaming can run after turns or compaction;
- session exit runs `SessionEnd` hooks, records telemetry/history, closes MCP, and exits.

Session exit path: [`src/cli/app/AppCoordinator.tsx#L3913-L3945`](https://github.com/letta-ai/letta-code/blob/d5d9263a404fbfbc08798eca5e87cb014a763b64/src/cli/app/AppCoordinator.tsx#L3913-L3945).

Post-turn synchronization:

- refuses to push dirty repos;
- pushes clean ahead commits;
- on non-fast-forward, performs `pull --rebase` and retries push;
- reports conflict rather than silently resetting.

Source: [`src/agent/memory-git.ts#L1957-L2096`](https://github.com/letta-ai/letta-code/blob/d5d9263a404fbfbc08798eca5e87cb014a763b64/src/agent/memory-git.ts#L1957-L2096).

# 6. Multi-agent and shared blocks

## Classic shared blocks

Classic sharing is literal row sharing:

```text
agent A ─┐
         ├── block-123
agent B ─┘
```

An update by either agent changes the same block and triggers system-prompt rebuilds for every connected agent. This is suitable for a small, always-in-context shared state, but it implies:

- one global character budget;
- one global `read_only` setting;
- one label per attached agent;
- concurrent writers need optimistic locking or stronger merge semantics;
- every update causes prompt invalidation/recompilation across all surfaces.

Groups also have a `groups_blocks` relation, and group setup attaches each shared block to every participant/manager agent: [`letta/orm/groups_blocks.py`](https://github.com/letta-ai/letta/blob/ff19ffeafeb54bd2a7dc5d4a552f10191732a235/letta/orm/groups_blocks.py), [`letta/services/group_manager.py#L400-L440`](https://github.com/letta-ai/letta/blob/ff19ffeafeb54bd2a7dc5d4a552f10191732a235/letta/services/group_manager.py#L400-L440).

## Current shared-memory direction

The current docs explicitly call shared blocks legacy:

> “Older Letta API guides use shared memory blocks for one in-context memory block attached to multiple agents. The legacy memory block API still supports this pattern, but users should migrate to shared memory repositories instead.”

Source: [`concepts/shared-memory/index.md#L6-L15`](https://github.com/letta-ai/letta-docs-md/blob/663d5afb3b902e3c24de6675810c85b7da816b64/concepts/shared-memory/index.md#L6-L15).

Current shared memory is an organization-owned Git repository cloned beside each agent’s MemFS:

```text
$MEMORY_DIR/../<repository-name>/
```

Agents edit with file/Git tools, commit, push, and other agents pull: [`concepts/shared-memory/index.md#L17-L27`](https://github.com/letta-ai/letta-docs-md/blob/663d5afb3b902e3c24de6675810c85b7da816b64/concepts/shared-memory/index.md#L17-L27).

### Implication for “one memory, many surfaces”

For a per-professor memory used by many prompt surfaces, the classic block model is actually closer to the requirement than Letta Code’s shared Git repositories:

- one canonical professor row/document;
- many surfaces reference its ID;
- compile it afresh per request;
- writes affect all future surfaces.

The important distinction is to share **the source memory entity**, not copied prompt strings. Prompt strings should be generated views/cache artifacts.
